sections.h2: Where to search Escambia County records
sections.html:
Deeds and other recorded land documents live on the Clerk's Landmark Web official records site. Tax and value data sit on the Property Appraiser and Tax Collector sites. Landmark Web searches by name, document, case number, book and page, consideration, record date, clerk file number and legal description.

The appraiser's site, escpa.org, covers parcels in Escambia County, the City of Pensacola and the Town of Century, with values from the 2026 certified roll. The Tax Collector's site finds a tax account by name, address or account number. Parcel data on the appraiser's site is not survey quality, so hire a surveyor when boundaries matter.

sections.h2: Older records at the Clerk's Public Records Center
sections.html:
The Clerk's Public Records Center holds court, board and marriage records, along with historical files that can only be viewed in person. They come in handy for old titles and family land.

  • Circuit civil files from 1820 to 1985
  • The Government Survey of 1827
  • Marriage books from 1822 to 1999
  • Old wills and will books from the 1800s
  • Probate cases from 1883 to 1997
  • The Spanish Census of Pensacola, 1820

Online court records require registration, and the Clerk's page links to a registration agreement form and a search guide. Mortgage foreclosure sales in Escambia County are listed on the Clerk's Online Public Records page.

Recording charges follow a statewide schedule under section 28.24, so the Pensacola clerk charges what clerks elsewhere in Florida do. The base is $5.00 for page one, $4.00 for every page after, and $1.00 for each name beyond the fourth.

Clerk recording charges, Florida Statutes s. 28.24(13)
ChargeAmount
First page$5.00
Each added page$4.00
Each name beyond four$1.00
Records modernization fund, first page$1.00
Records modernization fund, each added page$0.50
Added technology charge$4 per page

Page size and the number of names change the total, so call the Clerk for the current amount on your document. Deed stamp tax is paid at the same counter.

sections.h2: Check the record before you list
sections.html:
Pull your vesting deed and every recorded document under your name before the house goes on the market. Landmark Web lets you trace how title reached you by name, book and page, record date or legal description.

  • Confirm the legal description on your last deed matches the tax account on the Property Appraiser's site.
  • Look for recorded mortgages, liens or court documents that a payoff must clear.
  • Make sure each owner's name is spelled the same way on every instrument.
  • Note whether the parcel is inside Pensacola, Century or the unincorporated county, since that changes which non-ad valorem charges show on the tax bill.

Your title agent will run the same search. Finding a problem yourself leaves time to fix it before a buyer's deadline.

sections.h2: Documentary stamp tax on a deed
sections.html:
Escambia deeds carry the standard Florida rate of 70 cents on each $100 of price. Only Miami-Dade has a lower rate.

Price includes cash, a discharged obligation and any mortgage on the property, whether or not the buyer assumes it. Every party to the deed is liable no matter who agrees to pay, and the clerk collects the tax when the deed is recorded. Mortgages and notes run 35 cents per $100 secured, capped at $2,450 on a note, with no cap on a mortgage.

  • Warranty, special warranty, quit claim, trustee's and life estate deeds are taxable.
  • A deed given instead of foreclosure and an agreement for deed are taxable too.
  • A personal representative's deed under a probated will is not taxable.
  • A spousal homestead deed, where the only consideration is a mortgage, and a divorce deed for the marital home are exempt.

A deed conveying land must be in writing and signed in front of two witnesses. Section 689.01 calls for two subscribing witnesses, requires no seal and allows witnessing by audio-video technology.

Go over these points with your title agent before anything reaches the Clerk:

  • The legal description matches the prior recorded deed.
  • Every owner on record signs, and two witnesses sign for each.
  • Stamp tax is figured on the right price.
  • An attorney has reviewed any lady bird deed. In one Department of Revenue advisement, such a deed passed no present beneficial interest and drew no stamp tax on those facts, but other facts can change the result.

sections.h2: Protecting a property from fake deeds
sections.html:
Sign up for Property Fraud Alert on the Clerk's Landmark Web site. It emails a subscriber each time a land records document is recorded under a name they follow.

The service is free. It only reports recorded instruments and does not stop fraud. Still, an alert on your own name, and on the name of a deceased relative if you inherited the house, gives early warning of a forged deed. If an owner of family property has died and records were never updated, probate or another process may be needed to settle who owns it.

Each office keeps its own record. Tax history is with the Tax Collector, where taxes turn delinquent April 1 and a tax certificate can follow. Foreclosure sales run through the Clerk. Florida's sale statute has the clerk sell between 20 and 35 days after final judgment, with a 5 percent deposit from the high bidder.

For a house with probate history, ask the Public Records Center, which holds probate cases back to 1883 for in-person viewing. Florida allows summary administration when the non-exempt estate is $150,000 or less, or the decedent died more than two years earlier.

These records help when a signer's name changed or an heir must be proved. Marriage records from 1996 to the present are in the Public Records Center, and older books run back to 1822.

  • Marriage books: 1822 to 1999, viewed in person.
  • Microfiche: 1919 through 1995, plus indexes covering 1821 to 1900 and 1901 to 1918.
  • Records from 1996 forward: available through the Clerk's records service.

If your name differs between the vesting deed and your current ID, collect the marriage or court record that links the two names before you list. Otherwise the buyer's title company may stall the closing.

On closing day, bring photo ID and expect to sign the deed in front of the required witnesses. The title agent sends the signed deed to the Clerk for recording, and the stamp tax goes in with it.

faqs.q: Where are Escambia County deeds recorded?
faqs.a: At the county Clerk and Comptroller's office. Search recorded documents on the Clerk's Landmark Web site by name, book and page, record date and other fields.

faqs.q: What is the stamp tax on a deed in Escambia County?
faqs.a: 70 cents on each $100 of price, the statewide rate. All parties to the deed are liable, and the clerk collects it at recording.

faqs.q: How much is the first page recording fee in Florida?
faqs.a: $5.00 under section 28.24, plus $1.00 for the modernization fund and an added $4 per page technology charge. Each added page is $4.00 plus further charges.

faqs.q: Can I view Escambia County probate files from the 1800s online?
faqs.a: No. Old wills, probate cases from 1883 to 1997 and civil files from 1820 to 1985 can only be viewed at the Public Records Center.

faqs.q: Does Escambia County offer an alert for fraudulent deeds?
faqs.a: Yes. The Clerk's Property Fraud Alert emails you when a document is recorded under a name you follow. It is free but does not prevent fraud.
